label: Flattery
description: Praise aimed at your competence, expertise, or standing, offered to loosen your discretion before a follow-up question.
example: "You clearly know this program better than anyone in the room. Give me the two-minute version?"

label: Quid pro quo
description: An offer of a fact, favor, or personal disclosure made first, so you feel a social debt to reciprocate with information of your own.
example: "I'll tell you what I know about the merger if you tell me what your team's working on."

label: Provocation
description: Deliberate skepticism toward a claim you made, meant to draw out elaboration to prove it or an answer given out of irritation.
example: "I don't buy it. There's no way your team actually pulled that off."

label: Assumed knowledge
description: Speech that presumes you already know the sensitive detail, so confirming or correcting it feels like the natural response.
example: "So when the contract renewal falls through in March, what's the backup plan?"

label: The Scharff technique
description: A friendly, non-confrontational conversation that carries the impression the other person already knows most of it, drawing confirmation or denial without ever asking directly.
example: They talk about your program with total confidence, as if they already know it, and just wait for you to confirm it or let it stand.

label: False statement
description: An intentionally incorrect statement, offered so you supply the accurate version in the act of correcting it.
example: "I heard your project got canceled last spring."

label: Criticism
description: Criticism of your work, employer, or a rival, offered to draw a defensive rebuttal that reveals detail.
example: "Honestly, your team's approach seems way behind where the competition is."

label: One-upper
description: A modest or exaggerated claim shared first, meant to create a competitive pull to top it with a larger, more specific one.
example: "We shipped 200 units last quarter. Bet you didn't hit that."

label: Feigned ignorance
description: A pose of ignorance about a subject you know well, meant to draw out an explanatory answer aimed at a supposed novice.
example: "I have no idea how any of this works. Can you walk me through it like I'm new?"

label: Confidential bait
description: A disclosure framed as confidential, shared first so you feel invited to trade a confidence of your own.
example: "Just between us, my last project went way over budget too."

label: Good listener
description: Sustained, warm attention and active listening, used to keep you talking and steer the conversation toward a topic of interest.
example: They ask thoughtful follow-up after follow-up, always steering back to your work and never their own.

label: Mutual interest
description: A manufactured sense of shared interest or background, built quickly so cooperation and disclosure feel like a natural next step.
example: "Wait, you went to State too, and you work in defense? We have so much in common, tell me about your work."

label: Mirroring
description: Matching your body language, tone, and phrasing to build unconscious rapport that keeps the conversation open.
example: They mirror your posture and tone, then echo "so the schedule slipped, huh" every time timing comes up.

label: Bracketing
description: A deliberately wide or wrong numeric range, offered so you narrow it toward the true figure.
example: "I'd guess your budget is somewhere between two and five million. Closer to which end?"

label: Leading question
description: A question built around a hidden presumption, so any direct answer accepts a fact you never actually confirmed.
example: "So you're still having trouble with the vendor, right?"

label: Macro to micro
description: A conversation that opens broad, narrows to a single sensitive detail, then widens out again so the narrowing goes unnoticed.
example: Talk opens on the industry in general, narrows to your contract's exact timeline, then drifts back to small talk.

label: Oblique reference
description: Discussion of a related or comparable system, meant to draw you into using your own work as an unwitting reference point.
example: "The XYZ system handles that problem by doing X. Is that close to what you all do?"

label: Quote reported facts
description: A citation of already-public data, used as a springboard toward the unpublished detail that would confirm or extend it.
example: "The press release said the launch slipped to Q3, so I'm guessing the testing phase ran long?"

label: Word repetition
description: Your own key word or phrase, echoed back as a prompt for further elaboration on it.
example: You mention a "supply chain issue," and they repeat "supply chain issue..." and wait.

label: Direct question
description: A blunt, direct question that relies on the social norm that a question posed deserves an answer.
example: "What's your project's current budget and timeline?"

label: Questionnaire or survey
description: A survey or questionnaire that buries sensitive questions among benign ones under a plausible cover purpose.
example: A short survey on "industry trends" that slips in a question about your program's staffing levels.

label: Ruse interview
description: A fabricated interview, often posing as a recruiter or headhunter, staged to justify probing questions about recent work.
example: "I'm recruiting for a similar role. Tell me more about what you built on your last project."

label: Target associates
description: An approach routed through a relative or colleague, or questions about a group you do not belong to, to reach information indirectly.
example: "Your spouse mentioned you've been traveling a lot for work lately. Big project?"

label: Urge to complain
description: An invitation to vent about work frustration, used to surface setbacks, staffing gaps, and delays you would not otherwise volunteer.
example: "Sounds rough. What's actually going wrong with the schedule?"

label: Paper review
description: An unsolicited request to review a paper or proposal, framed to draw your sensitive expertise into the response.
example: "Would you mind reviewing this paper? It overlaps with what you're working on."

label: Offering assistance
description: Genuine, unsolicited help offered to you, used to surface your interests and needs and to build a sense of obligation.
example: "I know a guy who could fix that funding gap. What exactly are you short on?"

label: Hypothetical situation
description: A hypothetical scenario built directly on something you just said, inviting you to reason through sensitive ground as if it were speculation.
example: "So hypothetically, if that system did fail, what would the fallback look like?"

label: Setting manipulation
description: A deliberate shift of the conversation to a relaxed, off-work setting, sometimes involving alcohol, to lower your guard.
example: "Let's grab drinks somewhere quieter and keep talking about your work."

label: Disproportionate interest
description: One topic gets far more attention than the rest of the conversation, out of proportion to a normal exchange.
example: Every few minutes the conversation returns to your specific project, no matter what else came up in between.

label: Topic bridging
description: The conversation is deliberately steered from a neutral opener toward the subject they actually want.
example: Small talk about the weather turns, within two exchanges, into a question about your team's deadline.

label: Question density
description: An unusually high concentration of questions clustered on the same subject.
example: In a five-minute stretch, six of their questions all touch your program's budget or timeline.

label: Persistence and circling back
description: The same subject keeps returning to the conversation after you have moved past it.
example: You change the subject twice, and both times they find a way back to the same question.

label: Reformulation
description: A question you declined or deflected comes back reworded, testing whether a different phrasing gets an answer.
example: You dodge "what's your budget," and a few minutes later they ask "so is funding tight this year?"

label: Steering with mirroring
description: The conversation is actively steered toward a topic while the other person mirrors your tone and body language.
example: They match your energy and posture while gently walking every reply back toward your project.
